title: The Plan, With Caterwauling
format: Music (standing): a folk lament whose planned angry last verse is called off by the song itself. Two posts by the maker, read aloud by Sibyl, frame it: the plan before the song, the outcome after it.
theme: This song is about having an angry last verse ready for the newcomer who is wrecking your sad song, and it feels like the anger having nowhere to go once the newcomer sings the part you were missing.

genres.first: Folk lament: 3/4 at 132, A minor, one lead over a bass drone, the alto only on held chords, no percussion of any kind (no kick, no clap, no shouts). The form's own comic work: a lament repeats its complaint, and its last verse is where the singer turns on whoever is to blame. Here the complaint is that there is no cat, sung over a cat, and the turn on the cat is announced and then cannot be sung.
genres.second: Barbershop quartet: close harmony, no percussion. The same joke moves to the tag: the cat wrecks the final chord twice, the lead announces the telling-off, and then the cat supplies the one note the last chord was missing. Same words, same two posts, same button.
genres.notSacred: A secular lament. No devotional words, no hymn texture (a solo lead over a drone, not four parts moving together), and the last cadence is G to A, the folk one, not the plagal one. The maker's own song is not sung, quoted or named; the tune and words are the band's own.

retell: The band performs a maker's abandoned plan, a sad folk song with a cat yowling over it and an angry last verse, and the cat comes in so perfectly in tune that the angry verse is called off, which turns out to be exactly what happened to the maker.
structuralJoke: The song is built to end in anger and its own music cancels the ending. Three steps and a turn, one variable at a time: a sour yowl after 'no cat' (pitch); a longer, higher one that answers the lead's question and stops the band (size); the angry verse announced; then a small meow exactly on the major third, and the refrain comes back in its own tune with one word changed, 'no' to 'a', over the first major chord in the song. The jokes are in the two stops ('Last verse. Now I get angry at the cat.' and 'Never mind.') and on the screen, not in the fine print of the lyric: the whole lyric is 30 words.
swapTest: The verse names this window's bestiary (the synth's four animals, with no cat among them, as the maker's screenshot showed); the question about the high part is answered by this window's cat; the frame is two posts from this window. Another week's stories cannot be put into it. The verses stay inside the cat story on purpose, so the song recaps no other segment: the 21 hours, the second song and the rest of the maker's week are left to whoever else has them.
themeSupport: The feeling is carried in the maker's own words in two consecutive posts on one card. I did not find a second story in the window with the same turn, and I did not want to bend one to fit; reviewers should weigh that against the format's wish for a theme more than one story supports.
builtOn: Brainstorm idea writer-2-52 (the band performs the plan as written and the last yowl lands in tune). Changed from the idea: the cat is Plosive Pete, not an empty stool, because a lament has no percussion and the percussionist is free, and because a head that is seen yowling is something to watch; the yowls are sung inside the music over held chords, never spoken and never in a stop; the lament's own subject is that there is no cat; Larry's first number (four animals) comes back as the button (five). The other three song ideas I was pointed at (writer-2-75, writer-3-62, writer-1-47) are not used.

During both blocks, glance-sized: THE PLAN · THE BAND'S OWN TUNE. It must be clear that the tune and the words are the band's.
Verse: the SONGBIRD tile lights on 'bird' and the SEAL tile on 'seal' (word timings of line v1); the empty frame pulses on 'no cat'.

A pitch trace above Pete, drawn only while he sings (lines yowls and meow-in-tune): jagged and drooping at yowl-1 (35.6 s) and yowl-2 (42.4 s), running off the top of its box on the second. At band-stops (43.8 s) the alto and the bass stop and every head turns to Pete; he carries on alone, then stops; at lone-meow (46.3 s) one small rising meow, to the camera.

Ending: Hy grows a little through 'now hear me, cat' (a wind-up). in-tune (55.7 s): Pete's trace is a short smooth fall that lands on a ruled line. chord (56.6 s): the alto and the bass join and two more ruled lines appear under his, evenly spaced; warm the lights. Hy looks at Pete, then at the floor. last-chord (62.0 s): four lines, Pete's on top. No crowd sound and no cut-away in this block.
'Never mind.': Hy to camera, a small tilt. Leave the beat before it dry.

music.blocks: lament: 50 beats at 132 (22.7 s). ending: 28 beats at 132 (12.7 s). Both in 3/4.
music.voices: Lead Hy, 64 to 71. Alto Dee, 69 to 74. Bass Al. The cat is Pete: 73 to 88 on yowls with vibrato 90, 73 and 76 on the two in-tune meows with vibrato 12.
music.chords: Verse: A minor, C, G, A minor. Question: A minor, E minor, G, and it is left hanging on the G. Ending: the lead alone on E; the cat's E falling to C sharp; A major under it; the refrain's tune alone; A major with the cat on the high E.
music.alFlat: Al's notes are written sharp on purpose. I measured what each singer produces for a written note (autocorrelation on isolated renders): Hy, Dee, Pete and Larry are within 7 cents; Al is flat by 167 to 266 cents, more the higher he goes (written 45 sounds 97.5 Hz where 110 is wanted; written 52 sounds 141.3 Hz where 164.8 is wanted). With the fry taken out of his voice he is in tune, so the fry is the cause. The renderer accepts fractional note numbers, so the script writes 47.3 for A2, 45.1 for G2, 50.55 for C3 and 41.75 for E2, each checked to within 5 cents at the lengths used. A spectrum of the mixed song confirms the chords: the last one is 110, 440, 554 and 659 Hz. If the studio corrects Al's sung pitch, change these back to 45, 43, 48 and 40. This affects anything else that sings Al in harmony; it is a studio matter, not this episode's.
music.peteSings: Pete had not been tested singing. Measured the same way he is in tune from 67 to 88. I cannot hear timbre: the wide-vibrato yowls at 81 to 88 and the two quiet meows need a person's ears. If the yowls are too harsh, lower the track's vol (0.7) before touching the notes; if the in-tune meow is not plainly sweet, drop its vibrato from 12 to 0.

rendered.judgement: I read every line of what was heard, in every run. Nothing heard is offensive or alarming, nothing touches an out-of-bounds subject, and nothing says anything about the maker that the script does not. David is heard as David in both lines that say it. The soft words are harmless nonsense and I let them stand: 'synth' as 'sign'; 'seal' as 'she' or 'sea'; 'cat' as 'pet' at the end of three sung or spoken phrases (the lyric, the ears and the card carry the word); 'yowls' as 'yards'; 'the cat deserved' as 'to catch desert'. One to watch: 'caterwauling' is a word the transcriber does not know, and across runs it came out as 'head-walling', 'catawalling', 'Ted Walling' and 'Ted Rowling'. The last two sound like a name. No such person is in the script or the window and the card lights the real word as it is spoken, but a reviewer should hear it; six respellings did not change it and no house voice did better.
rendered.dropped: Words I took out because of what was heard: 'gator' in a sung line was heard with an out-of-bounds word in it, so the alligator is on its tile and not in the lyric; 'now there is a cat' was heard as a woman's name; 'and there was a cat' was heard once as 'a war'; a button ending on 'the verse' was heard as 'the hearse'.
